understood: why greedy works for activity selection (irrevocable choice never forecloses better future options)
why greedy fails for knapsack (locks in picks, can't undo for a better combination)
matrix chain multiplication subproblem definition (cheapest cost to multiply matrices i through j)
confused: visualizing two-dimensional (i,j) range subproblems versus one-dimensional item-count subproblems

questions.text: Is there a trick for holding (i,j) ranges in your head, or does everyone trip on that jump from 1D to 2D subproblems at first?
questions.why_teacher: This is a teaching/visualization trick built from watching many students hit this exact wall — not something derivable from the definition itself.
questions.tried: Correctly worked out the cost(i,j) formulation but said tracking two indices at once doesn't visualize as cleanly as counting items linearly.

questions.text: How do you tell upfront whether a new problem needs 2D range subproblems like matrix chain, or 1D ones like knapsack?
questions.why_teacher: Recognizing subproblem shape before solving is pattern-matching built from seeing many problems in practice, not something a definition can teach.
questions.tried: Correctly identified that matrix chain needs ranges while knapsack needs item counts, but couldn't say what tips you off to which one a new problem needs.
